strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: incorporating expert demonstrations during RL without destabilizing an instruction-tuned model. The proposed auxiliary loss is simple and supports separate supervised and RL prompt sets.

Table 1 reports promising improvements across two model families and task domains. CHORD-ϕ exceeds SFT-best+RL on AMC (62.5 versus 58.4) and MMLU-Pro (56.2 versus 51.3), while improving BFCL overall accuracy over pure RL (78.5 versus 77.1).

Includes useful comparisons with sequential SFT+RL, pure RL, LUFFY, and SASR, alongside training curves, response-length measurements, and scheduling ablations. The appendix provides several important training and evaluation settings.
weaknesses: The central objective has a consequential gradient ambiguity. Equation (4) explicitly stops gradients through its weights, but Equation (6) does not. Differentiating -p(1-p)log(p) through the weight can push low-probability expert tokens toward still lower probability, rather than merely down-weighting imitation. If detached weights are intended, this must be specified; otherwise the stated mechanism does not describe the actual objective.

The ablations do not adequately isolate token selection from loss-scale reduction. Since p(1-p) is at most 0.25 and often much smaller, CHORD-ϕ substantially reduces effective supervised influence at the same µ. Fixed-µ comparisons do not match this effective scale, and no benchmark-level comparison against p-only weighting or alternative normalized weights establishes the necessity of suppressing both probability extremes.

Evaluation selection is inconsistent: Section 4.1 explicitly defines SFT-best through test-set searches over learning rates and epochs, whereas Appendix A.2 says checkpoints are selected using validation data. The validation split and selection criterion are insufficiently specified. No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported; repeated evaluation samples do not address training variance, particularly for the modest AIME and BFCL improvements.

The largest generalization claim needs stronger evaluation controls. MMLU-Pro uses a math-specific system prompt and integer-index boxed answers, with original-model accuracy only 24.7%. Standard benchmark prompting and format-failure analysis are needed to distinguish improved general reasoning from improved compliance with the math-training output format.

Novelty is primarily an incremental weighting heuristic within an established supervised-plus-RL framework. Closely related SRFT and UFT are discussed but not evaluated. Starting from an instruction-tuned model is a relevant experimental setting, but does not itself establish a methodological distinction or justify excluding close methods.

Mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Entropy and reward curves, response lengths, and one elementary arithmetic case study do not establish selective acquisition of expert reasoning, preservation of foundational abilities, or exposure-bias reduction. Replacing unknown expert probabilities with one also makes the proposed importance weighting heuristic rather than a general correction for the expert trajectory distribution.

Scope and efficiency evidence remain limited: each task uses one policy model and the same expert family, with no controlled sweep over expert quality or distribution mismatch. Training-step curves do not establish compute efficiency when response lengths differ substantially, and total training cost and matched-compute comparisons are absent.

strengths: Addresses a relevant practical problem: incorporating expert demonstrations during RL without degrading an instruction-tuned model’s existing behavior. The auxiliary-loss design supports separate supervised and RL prompt sets.

Reports promising results across two model families and two task domains. CHORD-ϕ improves AMC from 58.4 to 62.5 and MMLU-Pro from 51.3 to 56.2 relative to SFT-best+RL, while achieving the highest reported BFCL overall score.
Provides useful training curves, response-length comparisons, fixed-versus-dynamic coefficient experiments, and implementation details covering rewards, prompts, and major hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central objective has a consequential gradient ambiguity. Equation (4) explicitly stops gradients through the weights, but Equation (6) does not. Differentiating through ϕ=p(1−p) does not simply reweight the SFT gradient: minimizing −p(1−p)log(p) can decrease an expert token’s probability when p is small. Whether the weights are detached must be specified, and the mathematical objective must match the implementation.

The ablations do not isolate token selection from reduced supervision strength. Since p(1−p)≤0.25, CHORD-ϕ substantially attenuates the auxiliary loss relative to unweighted SFT at the same µ. The fixed-µ comparisons do not match effective loss or gradient magnitudes. Comparisons against magnitude-matched constant weights, p-only weights, and alternative token-weighting functions are needed to establish the proposed mechanism.

Evaluation and checkpoint selection are insufficiently clear. Section 4.1 explicitly selects SFT-best using the test set across learning rates and epochs, whereas Appendix A.2 states that reported checkpoints are selected using validation data. The validation split and selection criterion are not adequately specified. No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported; repeated evaluation samples do not establish training robustness, particularly for small AIME and BFCL gains.

Novelty is limited relative to existing combinations of supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning. The main additions are a coefficient schedule and a simple probability-based weighting heuristic. Closely related SRFT and UFT are discussed but not evaluated. Starting from instruction-tuned models is a useful setting, but does not establish that competing methods cannot work there.

The causal interpretation exceeds the evidence. Accuracy dips, entropy curves, and one qualitative example do not establish that policy mismatch causes the proposed shift-readapt-overfit progression or that the method selectively transfers reasoning skills. Learning-rate effects, formatting adaptation, and response truncation remain plausible explanations. Setting unknown expert probabilities to one also yields a heuristic weighting scheme, rather than a generally valid importance-sampling correction.

The MMLU-Pro generalization claim needs stronger controls. Evaluation uses a math-specific system prompt, think tags, and boxed numeric option indices—the format directly reinforced during math training. Standard benchmark prompting and measurements of answer-format failures are needed to distinguish broader reasoning improvements from improved compliance with this evaluation format.

Claims of efficiency and broad robustness are not sufficiently demonstrated. There are no matched-compute comparisons or wall-clock/token-budget measurements despite large response-length differences and additional supervised updates. Each domain uses only one main policy model and the same expert family, and robustness to µ is supported primarily by training-reward curves rather than comprehensive held-out evaluations.

strengths: Addresses a practical problem: incorporating expert demonstrations into reinforcement learning without disrupting an instruction-tuned model’s existing behavior. The proposed auxiliary loss is simple and accommodates separate supervised and RL prompt sets.

Table 1 reports promising improvements across two model families and task domains. Compared with SFT-best+RL, CHORD-ϕ improves AMC from 58.4 to 62.5 and MMLU-Pro from 51.3 to 56.2; BFCL overall improves from 77.1 for pure RL to 78.5.

The paper includes relevant sequential and interleaved training baselines, training-dynamics plots, response-length measurements, and useful implementation details. Averaging multiple generations on the small mathematical benchmarks helps reduce evaluation sampling noise.
weaknesses: The central objective has a consequential gradient ambiguity. Equation (4) explicitly stops gradients through its weights, but Equation (6) does not. Differentiating through ϕ=p(1−p) introduces an additional term; minimizing −p(1−p)log(p) can decrease the probability of low-probability expert tokens, rather than merely attenuating their imitation gradients. The paper must specify the implemented gradient and reconcile it with its explanation. Loss normalization also changes from token averaging in Equation (1) to a trajectory-wise sum in Equation (6), leaving the effective mixing coefficient unclear.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed weighting principle from simply weakening supervision. Since p(1−p)≤0.25, applying ϕ substantially reduces the auxiliary loss. The fixed-weight experiments are useful, but there is no matched-loss or matched-gradient-scale comparison, and no benchmark-level comparison against p-only weighting or alternative weighting functions. Thus, the necessity of suppressing both probability extremes remains insufficiently demonstrated.

Evaluation reliability is incompletely established. Section 4.1 explicitly selects SFT-best using the test set, whereas Appendix A.2 states that checkpoints are selected using validation data; the validation split and selection criteria are not adequately specified. No independent training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported. Repeated evaluation samples do not address training variance, which matters for the relatively small AIME and BFCL gains.

The large MMLU-Pro improvement needs stronger evaluation controls. Appendix A.6 uses a math-specific system prompt, think tags, and boxed numerical option indices for a broad knowledge benchmark. This could conflate improved reasoning with improved compliance with the training format. Standard benchmark prompting and a breakdown of answer-extraction failures are needed to substantiate the generalization claim.

Novelty and positioning are not sufficiently established relative to existing hybrid SFT/RL and probability-weighted SFT methods. Closely related SRFT and weighted-SFT approaches are discussed but not directly evaluated. Starting from an instruction-tuned model is a useful setting, but does not by itself establish a substantial methodological distinction.

Several explanations exceed the evidence. Reward, entropy, and response-length curves do not establish that policy mismatch causes the full shift-readapt-overfit progression or that the method selectively acquires beneficial reasoning strategies. Controlled expert-mismatch experiments and quantitative reasoning-behavior analyses are missing. Likewise, efficiency claims lack wall-clock or compute-matched comparisons. These gaps, together with the objective ambiguity, leave the paper below the acceptance threshold despite its encouraging results.

strengths: Addresses a practical post-training problem: incorporating expert demonstrations without destabilizing an instruction-tuned model’s existing behavior.
The proposed probability-based token weighting is simple and inexpensive to implement, and permits separate supervised and RL prompt sets.
Table 1 reports meaningful improvements over strong sequential baselines, including AMC accuracy of 62.5 versus 58.4 and MMLU-Pro accuracy of 56.2 versus 51.3 for SFT-best+RL.

The evaluation includes math, tool use, and medical QA, with additional experiments on weaker models, an MoE model, alternative experts, weighting functions, and SRFT. Response-length and training-dynamics analyses provide useful context.
weaknesses: The central objective is materially underspecified. Equation 4 explicitly stops gradients through its weights, but Equation 6 does not. Differentiating through -p(1-p)log(p) can decrease the probability of unlikely expert tokens, contrary to the stated interpretation as down-weighted imitation. For example, its derivative with respect to p is positive at p=0.1. The paper must clarify the implemented gradient and reconcile the equations. Equation 6 also replaces Equation 1’s token normalization with a sequence expectation of token sums, leaving the effective loss balance ambiguous.

The experiments do not adequately isolate selective token weighting from simply reducing supervision strength. Since p(1-p) is at most 0.25, adding this weight substantially reduces the auxiliary loss. Although several fixed coefficients and alternative functions are evaluated, there is no control matched for average weight or gradient magnitude. The claimed mechanism therefore remains uncertain.

Statistical support is insufficient: no independent training-seed results or confidence intervals are reported. Multiple evaluation samples on AIME and AMC reduce decoding noise but do not address training variability. This particularly matters for the 1.3-point BFCL improvement over SFT-light+RL and approximately one-point AIME improvements over SFT-best+RL.

Checkpoint selection is inconsistent: Section 4.1 explicitly selects SFT-best using the test set, whereas Appendix A.2 says reported checkpoints are selected using validation data. Validation construction and method-specific tuning budgets are not sufficiently specified. The large MMLU-Pro gains also need a standard-prompt evaluation to separate general reasoning improvements from adaptation to the imposed math-oriented response format.

The causal explanation exceeds the evidence. Accuracy dips, entropy curves, response lengths, and selected examples do not establish that response-pattern mismatch causes degradation or that the method selectively acquires useful reasoning skills. Expert changes also change content and quality. Controlled style interventions and quantitative measurements of divergence, diversity, and token-level learning would strengthen these claims.

The methodological advance over existing hybrid SFT/RL objectives and probability-weighted supervision is relatively incremental. Its empirical justification needs stronger controls and reproducibility: exact selected hyperparameters, loss implementation, and matched compute comparisons are missing. Training-step curves and response lengths alone do not establish the claimed training efficiency when methods have different rollout lengths and auxiliary computation.

Table 1 reports meaningful improvements over SFT-best+RL on AMC (62.5 versus 58.4) and MMLU-Pro (56.2 versus 51.3), alongside smaller improvements on AIME and tool use.
The appendix substantially broadens the evaluation with alternative weighting functions, expert sources, weaker models, a MoE model, medical question answering, and an SRFT comparison.
Response-length and training-curve analyses provide useful observations about how expert imitation changes model behavior.
weaknesses: The central objective has a consequential gradient ambiguity. Equation 4 explicitly stops gradients through its weights, but Equation 6 does not. Differentiating -p(1-p)log(p) introduces an additional term and can decrease the probability of low-probability expert tokens, contrary to the stated interpretation of merely down-weighting imitation. The paper must specify whether weights are detached and establish that the reported experiments implement the intended objective.

The evaluation protocol is inconsistent and insufficiently specified. Section 4.1 selects SFT-best using the test set, whereas Appendix A.2 says reported checkpoints are selected using validation data. Validation construction and selection criteria are not adequately documented. No independent training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported; averaging multiple sampled answers does not address training variance, particularly for the small AIME and BFCL improvements.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate token selection from reduced supervision strength. Since p(1-p) is at most 0.25, introducing it substantially reduces the effective SFT contribution. Fixed-coefficient experiments partially address this, but there is no convincing comparison matching average weight or gradient magnitude. Moreover, Equation 6 uses a sequence sum while Equation 1 uses token normalization, leaving the effective loss scale unclear.

The novelty is narrower than the claimed unification of on-policy and off-policy learning. Combining supervised and RL objectives, scheduling their balance, and probability-weighting supervised tokens already appear in the cited literature. The principal distinction is the particular token-weighting heuristic; comparisons against directly related probability-weighted SFT approaches are insufficient to establish its incremental value.

The proposed explanation is stronger than the evidence. Accuracy dips, entropy curves, response lengths, and a selected elementary arithmetic example do not establish that policy-pattern disruption causes the observed degradation or that CHORD selectively transfers reasoning strategies. Controlled experiments separating expert style, correctness, length, and optimization strength are missing.

Claims of efficiency and broad robustness remain under-supported. Training steps are not matched compute when response lengths and additional supervised processing differ, and no wall-clock or token-budget comparison is provided. The medical extension compares primarily against pure RL using a model judge, while robustness to the global coefficient is supported mainly by a limited schedule comparison rather than a systematic sensitivity study.

strengths: Addresses a practical problem: incorporating expert demonstrations into instruction-tuned models without destabilizing their existing behavior. The auxiliary-loss formulation is simple and does not require matching expert prompts to RL prompts.
The main results are promising. CHORD-ϕ improves over pure RL from 52.1 to 62.5 on AMC, 45.8 to 56.2 on MMLU-Pro, and 77.1 to 78.5 on BFCL, and generally outperforms sequential SFT+RL.

The experimental coverage is substantial: mathematical reasoning, tool use, medical QA, multiple model families including an MoE model, and different expert sources. Comparisons include LUFFY, SASR, and an additional SRFT comparison in the appendix.
Useful ablations examine mixing schedules, alternative token weights, weaker policies, and response lengths. The entropy and reward curves provide supporting evidence for improved training stability.
weaknesses: The central objective has a consequential gradient ambiguity. Equation 4 explicitly stops gradients through its weight, whereas Equation 6 does not. Differentiating through p(1−p) introduces an additional term and can decrease the probability of low-probability expert tokens, rather than merely attenuating their imitation gradient. The implementation must clarify whether weights are detached. Equation 6 also changes from token-normalized SFT to a sequence-summed expression without explaining the normalization used experimentally.

The ablations do not fully separate selective token weighting from reducing the effective SFT strength. Since p(1−p) is at most 0.25, applying it substantially shrinks the auxiliary loss. The fixed-µ comparisons and alternative weighting functions are useful, but controls matching average weight or gradient magnitude are needed to establish that the proposed weighting shape drives the improvement.

Evaluation uncertainty and model selection are insufficiently documented. No repeated-training-seed statistics or confidence intervals are reported; repeated decoding on AIME does not measure training variance. Several gains over strong baselines are small. Section 4.1 describes SFT-best as selected on the test set, whereas Appendix A.2 says reported checkpoints are validation-selected; this inconsistency and the validation protocol require clarification.

The causal interpretation exceeds the evidence. Entropy curves, response lengths, and selected examples do not establish that policy-pattern disruption and overfitting cause the observed performance drops. Likewise, assigning an unknown behavior probability of one is a heuristic, not a generally valid importance-sampling correction. Controlled style-mismatch experiments and quantitative retention or diversity measurements would strengthen the explanation.

The conceptual novelty is narrower than the broad unification framing suggests: hybrid supervised/RL objectives and scheduled mixing already exist, leaving the particular token weighting as the main distinction. Efficiency claims lack matched-compute or wall-clock comparisons. The large MMLU-Pro gains also warrant a standard-prompt and answer-format control, since evaluation uses a math-specific prompt with integer-coded choices.
